  displacements - a suite releasing the slot is ordinary. This does not
  change how subscriptions are counted; it names which of the two candidate
  causes is in play the first time it happens, instead of leaving two
  symptoms that point nowhere. `test/subscription-accounting.test.js` installs
  a second sink and reads the displacement back, and holds the half that
  matters downstream: after a takeover the displaced counter stops moving at
  all, which is what strands a total.

- **The simulator reaches the attach regime, through the primary's own
  stamping and sweep.** `classifyWorkerHealth` judges a ready worker on its
  ready-to-attach gap only when the meta carries `readyAt` and
  `relayAttached` explicitly, and the simulator built its meta without them,
  so that branch was unreachable from any scenario. The two liveness steps the
  primary kept inline now live beside the classifier in `worker-watchdog.js`:
  `recordWorkerMessage` applies one inbound worker message to the slot record
  (the heartbeat clock every message advances, the ready edge under each
  cluster mode with its `readyAt`, the one-time `relay-attached` flip) and
  names the transition, and `sweepWorkerHealth` runs one heartbeat sweep over
  a cohort. index.js calls both; the simulator calls the sweep over metas that
  carry the same fields, and `attachFailWorker(id)` puts a worker into the
  ready-but-unattached state. Its ready edge does not reset the simulated
  budget - the primary stamps the budget on the attach - so a worker that
  fails to attach on every boot exhausts in the simulator as it does in
  production. Deliberately not modelled: the consequence of the state (the
  unattached worker's subscribers missing every cross-worker publish), which
  is evidence about the failure rather than the watchdog and would need the
  relay bus to gate on the flag; the real cluster tests cover that path.

- **How the attach regime is held on both sides.** The unit suite drives the
  primary's composition end to end: slot records shaped as `spawn_worker`
  builds them, messages posted in the order a worker posts them with the
  attach withheld, the shared sweep, and the real restart supervisor charging
  the exit - the unattached slot's attempts climb across two lives while the
  attached sibling resets, and a deterministic attach failure walks to
  exhaustion. The attach-gate pins hold the flip to the shared function and
  the primary to routing every message through it. The simulator cases cover
  the escalation and recovery, the inside-the-window boundary, a disabled
  boot deadline (the regime is not tied to it) and a worker whose every
  respawn fails to attach, each replaying reproducibly. The golden corpus is
  re-blessed: a run's fingerprint folds its metrics object, so the added
  `attachFailures` key moves every fingerprint, and the corpus verified
  against a build with only that key removed matched 40 of 40 - the behaviour
  under every recorded seed is unchanged.

- **The control/ack channel is bounded per connection.** Everything on it
  shares a property ordinary fan-out does not: the client asked for it. A
  subscribe buys an ack, a bad frame buys a refusal, an oversized batch buys a
  denial for every topic past the cap. So the channel amplifies, and measured
  at the worst legal shape it amplifies twelvefold - one 8,121-byte
  `subscribe-batch` of 1,344 shortest-legal topics is answered with 97,484
  bytes across 1,345 frames.
  Nothing covered it. The control-frame limit bounds one frame, which bounds
  the frame count per inbound frame but not the rate; every `messageAdmission`
  ceiling normalizes to zero when the option is absent, so out of the box there
  is no inbound rate at all; the publish-egress ceilings meter application
  publishes and never see an ack; and `maxBackpressure` bounds the queue in
  MEMORY, which is why this was a CPU and bandwidth problem rather than an
  out-of-memory one.
  Each connection now carries a 4 MiB budget over a 10-second window, and one
  that exceeds it is closed rather than served. Every control frame the runtime
  emits goes through one `sendControl`, so there is no longer a raw `ws.send`
  on that path to forget to charge - the binary game lane's `game-denied` and
  the `wire-id` announces included, which live in modules shared across the
  surfaces and therefore take the calling surface's sender as an argument
  rather than reaching for a socket. Frames are charged at their UTF-8 size,
  which is what leaves on the wire, and the exhaustion event carries the
  connection's request id so the client can be found in the access log.

- **What that ceiling is worth, and why it closes.** The number is derived
  rather than picked: a reconnecting client restores in batches of at most 256
  topics and is answered with about 15 KB, a 5,000-topic restore costs about
  300 KB, and the budget sits roughly 270 times above the first - while the
  amplifier reaches it from about 34 KB/s of sustained inbound, a rate no real
  client produces on a channel that is bursty at reconnect and quiet after.
  Closed rather than shed, because an ack the client never receives is a
  subscription it believes did not take - the exact failure the loud per-topic
  denial exists to prevent, so shedding would trade an amplifier for a
  correctness bug.
  NOTHING NEW GOES ON THE WIRE. The close is 4429, already this client's
  THROTTLE class, so it reconnects on the accelerated curve; an explanatory
  `error` frame would have meant a new `code` value and a field the documented
  error shape does not carry, which is a wire change and the protocol is frozen
  at revision 1. The operator is told through
  `ADAPTER-ERR-CONTROL-EGRESS-EXHAUSTED` instead, and
  `test/control-egress.test.js` pins the silence so a later helpful frame is
  caught as the wire change it would be. It drives the real runtime from both
  ends: the amplifier is cut, and a twenty-batch resubscribe is not.

### Changed

- **One connection holds at most 65,536 subscriptions.**
  `MAX_SUBSCRIPTIONS_PER_CONNECTION` was a million like the other retained-state
  caps, on the position that per-connection caps are bug tripwires and the
  connection ceiling bounds the aggregate. That position holds only while one
  connection is cheap, and a landed subscription is not: it is a native uWS
  topic-tree entry as well as a Set entry and a string, measured on the test
  server at about 706 bytes of resident memory each (20,000 landed
  subscriptions on one connection, 13.4 MB RSS delta, 94 bytes of it heap). At
  the old cap one admitted connection could hold about 700 MB, which
  `maxConnections` cannot see, and the control-egress budget throttles the
  fill only to roughly 80,000 acks per ten seconds, so a hostile client reached
  it in minutes. The new cap is about 46 MB at worst per connection and
  sixty-four times a thousand-topic client. The refusal path, the reason code
  and the surfaces are unchanged; only the constant moves, and the caps table
  in the README says why this one row is not a million.
- **Four metric help strings name what is counted, not the layer that counted
  it.** `ws_publishes_total` said "fan-out happens in C++",
  `ws_publish_outcomes_total` said "Native publish calls", and the two dropped
  counters said "dropped by the native backpressure limit". A `# HELP` line is
  what an operator reads to interpret a number, and naming the runtime in it
  makes the sentence require knowledge of the implementation to parse - and
  makes it untrue anywhere the same manifest is served by a backend that fans
  out and sheds in JavaScript. The meanings are unchanged: "never
  per-recipient deliveries" and "dropped under backpressure" say the same
  thing without the layer.
  The declaration in `src/index.d.ts` is where this adapter's specifics
  belong, and it now carries one that is easy to meet on a dashboard first: a
  publish that EXCLUDES a socket is delivered by a per-socket walk rather than
  one native `app.publish`, so it is counted by `ws_publishes_total` and does
  not appear in the outcome breakdown. The two counters therefore do not sum,
  by construction rather than by accident - the breakdown counts native
  fan-out calls, and an excluding publish is not one.

- **A `subs.total-mismatch` violation carries the two counts that say which
  defect produced it.** The context gained `connections`, the number of
  connections the sum came from, and `settled`, how many of those carried a
  registry the close path had already released. A membership charged twice and
  a closed connection still enumerated in the live set raise `summed` against
  an unchanged total identically, so the sum alone could not tell them apart -
  `settled` above zero means topics the counter has given up are still being
  summed, and zero rules that out and points at the memberships instead.
  `isSettledSubscriptionRegistry` (utils/ws-symbols.js) reads the WeakSet the
  close path already marks; `buildConnectionAuditSnapshot` takes it as an
  injected predicate rather than importing it, so the builder still reads
  nothing but its arguments and a caller that cannot answer omits the count
  instead of reporting a zero it did not measure.
  `test/invariants.test.js` and `test/auditor-snapshot.test.js` hold both
  arms, including that an absent predicate leaves the field off.

- **The `seq` option resolves through one table on every lane and surface.**
  `stampSeq` used to key on two types and let everything else fall through to
  the counter - including `null` from a nullable column and `'1234'` from a
  JSON round trip, both of which silently marked the topic non-authoritative.
  The table is now total: number and bigint are the explicit authority
  (validated by one shared `explicitSeqValue`, which holds both spellings to
  the safe-integer range the IEEE-double seq space carries unchanged, and
  refuses anything past it rather than rounding two ids onto one seq),
  `true` and absent draw the counter, `false` and `null` omit the seq, and
  anything else throws the legal forms. `publishWireBatch` entries resolve through the same table via
  a shared `resolveEntrySeq`, which also ends two silent entry-lane quirks:
  an entry could not opt OUT of a batch-level counter (`seq: false` fell
  through to the shared options), and a non-number entry seq published the
  entry under whatever the options said. The resolver is one function used
  by production, `createTestServer`, and the Vite dev plugin, so the three
  surfaces cannot drift, and its refusals name the offending entry position -
  one bad value refuses the whole batch, so a caller passing hundreds needs
  more than the value back; `test/batch-sequence-mirror-parity.test.js` holds
  the acceptance and refusal table against the mirrors, and
  `test/seq-stamp.test.js` the resolver itself.

### Fixed

- **A request may say where its body ends only once, and only in a way this
  server and the one in front of it read alike.** Measured against the
  pinned uWebSockets.js: the parser refuses `Content-Length: 0x6`, `+6` and
  `6abc`, and refuses a request carrying both `Transfer-Encoding` and
  `Content-Length`, but it reads the PRESENCE of `Transfer-Encoding` rather
  than its value - `xchunked`, `chunkedX`, `gzip`, `chunked, chunked`,
  `gzip, chunked` and `chunked, gzip` are all decoded as chunked - and it
  accepts an empty `Content-Length`. A conformant intermediary reads an
  unknown coding as one it cannot frame a body with, so it forwards the
  request as bodyless and treats what follows as the next request, while
  this server consumes those same bytes as a chunked body. That disagreement
  is what a smuggled request is made of, so the adapter answers these shapes
  itself: `Transfer-Encoding` must be exactly `chunked` (RFC 9112 6.1 allows
  the coding at most once and only as the final one, and this server decodes
  no other), `Content-Length` must be a bare decimal count, and neither may
  arrive twice. `framingRefusal` in `src/runtime/utils/request-headers.js`
  holds the rule, and it is asked twice over. One lookup,
  `transfer-encoding`, runs in front of EVERY route - wrapped around the
  registrations rather than written into a handler, so the lanes that answer
  before acting on any header set (a built asset, a prerendered page, the
  health and readiness probes, the waiting room's own pages) are covered by
  the same line as the rest. The doors that read the whole header set and
  act on it then ask the whole rule, so SSR, authenticate, admin and the
  handshake also see a framing header sent empty or sent twice.
- **The handshake asks it for itself.** A WebSocket route takes an options
  object rather than a handler, so the wrapper never sees it, and the siege,
  over-capacity and connection-capacity answers in front of the upgrade all
  keep their connections. An ambiguously framed handshake arriving at a full
  gate would have been answered 503 on a connection whose remaining bytes
  are the ones in dispute, so the upgrade callback asks the same one lookup
  before any of them. A repeat of any other single-valued header no longer
  masks a framing one either: the framing answer is returned first, because
  only it says the connection can no longer be read.
- **What that one lookup does not reach, and why the line is there.** A
  header lookup answers the empty string for an absent header and for one
  sent empty alike, and returns the first of a repeated one, so it cannot
  see those two shapes; a lane that never builds a header set still serves
  them. The alternatives were measured against the built static lane in
  `bench/39-request-framing-guard-ab.mjs`. A walk of the header list - the
  only form that sees an empty or repeated framing header - costs about 8%
  of that answer, and an integer compare on the key length ahead of the
  string compare buys none of it back. A lookup form costs at most a few
  percent, and on the quietest host measured it sat inside the control arm's
  own drift. Closing those two shapes in front of every route would be paid
  by every asset request forever, so they are closed where the header set is
  read and acted on anyway, and left open where the answer comes first. A
  case in `test/request-framing-real.test.js` pins the served answer, so the
  line cannot move without a run saying so.
- **A framing refusal closes the connection.** RFC 9112 6.3: a 400 that
  keeps reading leaves the ambiguous bytes in place for the next parse, so
  the refusal ends the connection, and uWS writes the `Connection: close`
  that says so (the adapter writes none of its own, which would put the
  field on the wire twice). Scoped to the two headers that frame a body, so
  a repeated `Authorization` is still answered on a connection that stays
  open, which `test/request-framing-real.test.js` pins beside the refusals. The handshake door separates the two in its own counter as well:
  `ambiguous_framing` where the body boundary is in question,
  `duplicate_header` where it is not.
- **A HEAD request takes the headers and no payload.** uWS writes whatever
  `end()` is handed, and a client stops reading a HEAD response at the
  header terminator (RFC 9112 6.3), so bytes written after it stayed in the
  connection buffer and were parsed as the start of the next response on a
  keep-alive connection. `curl -I` closes the connection and never showed
  it. Two lanes wrote such bytes. The generated errors: a 405 on the
  authenticate path, a 400 from the request edge, a 500 from the SSR failure
  path and the admin lane's JSON errors and handler bodies all went through
  `end(text)`. And SvelteKit itself: its endpoint lane routes HEAD to the
  GET handler and hands that Response back unchanged, pages render in full,
  and dropping the body is left to the server, which node:http does for
  adapter-node and uWS does not. The helpers in `http-helpers.js` take a
  HEAD flag and finish through `endWithoutBody(text.length)`, so
  `Content-Length` still names the entity size; the admin writers do the
  same for a handler body; the SSR writer never reads a HEAD body, reports a
  declared `Content-Length` and otherwise sends no framing header,
  cancelling the stream. A 413 takes no flag: it answers a request body,
  which a HEAD never carries. `createTestServer`'s admin mirror follows.
  `test/head-and-204-framing-real.test.js` pins it over raw sockets: a
  second request pipelined behind the HEAD must begin exactly at the header
  terminator, and for the endpoint a lone HEAD read through EOF must end at
  it.
- **A 204 reports no Content-Length; a 304 only a declared one.** Bodyless
  responses finished through `endWithoutBody(0)` - the implicit authenticate
  success, the SSR writer (SvelteKit's OPTIONS answer and its ETag 304 among
  them) and the admin writers - or through `end()`, which writes the same
  zero: a 204 `Response` an authenticate hook returns, and the static lane's
  304. RFC 9110 8.6 forbids the header on a 204, and permits it on a 304
  only when it names the length of the 200's content, which a zero for a
  rendered page never does.
  `endBodyless(res, status, declaredLength, headOnly)` in `http-helpers.js`
  holds the rule: a 204 reports nothing, a
  304 and a HEAD only the length the Response declared (the header may name
  only the GET's content length, which the Response carries when SvelteKit
  declared it for a rendered page or an app answering HEAD itself set it),
  every other bodyless response zero - a declared length with no bytes
  behind it would leave the client waiting for them, which the SSR writer
  used to allow. Reported without a length, uWS emits neither
  `Content-Length` nor `Transfer-Encoding` and still completes the exchange,
  which the same suite proves by pipelining a request behind each 204 and
  304, the built runtime's admin lane 204 included.
- **The error reference links the extensions repository's errors document
  where it ships.** `svelte-adapter-uws-extensions` carries it at
  `docs/errors.md`, the path `svelte-realtime` uses too, and `docs/errors.md`
  here links that path.
- **`vite dev` no longer withholds an echo that production delivers.** The dev
  plugin read `options.excludeWs` on `platform.publish`, and through it on
  `batch` and on the per-event fall-back `publishBatched` takes for a disjoint
  batch, while production reads no exclusion on any of those: that lane is one
  native fan-out, and skipping a single socket means falling back to a
  per-connection walk. An app developed against the dev server saw the sender
  suppressed and got the echo under `npm start`, with nothing to notice in
  between - and dev was not even consistent with itself, since the batched
  fast path never excluded. Exclusion
  stays declared and implemented where the walk already lives - `publishWire`
  and `publishWireBatch` - and those honour it in dev exactly as before. In
  production the same option also covers the envelope a codec falls back to
  when it declines a frame, which is the supported way to skip the sender
  without a binary payload.
- **`vite dev` refuses the seq values production refuses.** The dev plugin
  stamps no `seq` and read none on `platform.publish`, so `{ seq: 'x' }`, a
  zero, a negative or a fraction delivered under `vite dev` and threw a
  `TypeError` under `npm start`. Every dev lane now runs the value check
  production runs before it admits - `publish` and the wire lanes through the
  delivery seam, `batch` and `publishBatched` over every message before the
  first goes out - so a bad value throws the same error on both servers, with
  nothing of a batch delivered. The publish lanes in dev still stamp no seq on
  the values they accept; the send lanes carry an explicit one as before.
- **A JSON array no longer reaches the app hook as a pre-parsed envelope.**
  `MessageContext.msg` is declared to carry a plain object envelope and to be
  absent for null, an array and a primitive, but the runtime tested
  `parsed === null || typeof parsed !== 'object'` and `typeof [] === 'object'`:
  a frame such as `[{"y":1}]` parsed, matched no control type, and arrived at
  the app hook as `msg`. `createTestServer` and `vite dev` already excluded
  arrays by name, so an app saw one envelope shape in development and another
  in production. The runtime now excludes it the same way; the frame still
  reaches the hook, as raw `data` with no envelope beside it.
- **A shared cohort join holds one reference and leaves the connection in one
  cohort.** `joinSharedCohort` acquired a shared wire-id reference on every
  call while membership is a Set, so a plugin's `trackedSubscribe` of a socket
  the client already held over the wire took a reference the single leave
  released once: the id outlived its last member, the egress split
  over-counted the binary cohort, and every later publish built a binary frame
  for nobody. A join of a topic the connection already holds now acquires
  nothing and announces nothing. The same call could also leave a connection
  on BOTH cohorts - its own first announce refused past the backpressure limit
  put it on the JSON cohort, and a later successful join added the binary one
  without removing that - so it received every shared publish twice, as the
  frame and as the envelope; the successful join now moves the connection
  rather than adding to it, and a join that finds the capability gone - a
  re-sent `hello` replaces the set, a refused per-connection announce poisons
  the wire state - moves it the other way, out of the binary cohort and off
  its reference. Both in the runtime and in `createTestServer`.
  `ws_publish_outcomes_total` is unchanged and stays per native call: a publish
  that splits its topic into cohorts makes one native call per cohort it
  publishes to and reports one outcome for each, so a `no_subscribers` there
  answers for one cohort and not for the publish. That is now stated where the
  metric is documented rather than left to be discovered.
- **A failing `unsubscribe` hook no longer takes the worker or the message
  handler with it.** The hook is fire-and-forget and was invoked bare at
  thirty sites across the runtime, the test server and the dev plugin, so an
  async hook's rejection was an unhandled rejection - fatal under Node's
  default policy - and a synchronous throw propagated into the message
  handler. One helper now invokes it everywhere: a throw is caught, a
  returned thenable gets a rejection handler, and either failure is reported
  once as `ADAPTER-ERR-UNSUBSCRIBE-HOOK` with the topic and the connection's
  request id. The contract is unchanged - the promise is still not awaited, so
  no in-flight set and no bound appear - and the connection keeps its other
  subscriptions. Pinned on the helper, the test server and the built runtime
  over a real socket, throw and rejection both; the fixture's hook selects
  the failure by topic name.
- **`bytes=-0` is answered 416, not with the whole body.** The range parser
  read a zero-length suffix as malformed, and a malformed Range is ignored, so
  a request for the last zero bytes got a 200 with everything. RFC 9110 14.2
  makes a suffix range satisfiable only with a non-zero length; the parser
  (`utils/byte-range.js`, moved out of the static handler so the suite drives
  the served line rather than a transcription of it) now reports it
  unsatisfiable, and the static lane answers `416` with
  `Content-Range: bytes */N` against the negotiated representation's length.
- **A 304 carries the app's configured headers.** The revalidation response
  was assembled from four named fields (`ETag`, `Vary`, `Cache-Control`,
  `Last-Modified`), so every `staticHeaders` entry - HSTS, CSP, frame and
  referrer policy - was absent on every revalidation, and a client that
  revalidates on each navigation saw its security policy once. The 304 now
  writes the representation's 200 header tuples - validators, caching
  directives and every configured entry; `Content-Type` is written only beside
  a body - less the fields that describe the body it does not carry
  (`Content-Encoding`, `Content-Disposition`; RFC 9110 15.4.5), baked per
  representation at index time so the revalidation path stays one loop.
- **Accept-Encoding is negotiated by its weights, not by substring.** Both the
  static lane and the single-chunk SSR lane chose a coding with
  `includes('br')` then `includes('gzip')`, so `br;q=0` - a refusal - was
  served brotli, `gzip;q=1, br;q=0.5` got brotli, and a bare `*` got
  identity. `utils/content-coding.js` reads the list as RFC 9110 12.5.3 does:
  an unlisted coding is acceptable only through `*`, `q=0` refuses, the
  highest weight wins and brotli breaks a tie; identity stays the fallback
  even under `identity;q=0`. The browser shape (brotli listed weightless) is
  decided by one substring search; measured on the static and SSR lanes under
  autocannon, the change sits inside the control arm's spread
  (`bench/38-content-coding-lanes-ab.mjs`).
- **A prerendered trailing-slash redirect is percent-encoded.** The lookup
  matches the DECODED path and wrote it verbatim into `Location`, so a
  prerendered route with a non-ASCII name redirected with the name's raw UTF-8
  bytes in the header - and a client sending the bytes raw in its request line
  got them back the same way. The target is now spelled as a request target
  (`utils/location-target.js`), path segments and query alike, so the redirect
  lands on the lookup that issued it. Pinned against the built runtime over a
  raw socket, encoded and raw-byte spellings both.
- **On Windows, the reserved-character refusal reads the decoded path too.**
  The gate that answers 400 to a path naming an NTFS alternate data stream
  (`:`) or an 8.3 short name (`~`) read the raw request target only, so
  `/x%3Ay` passed a gate that refused `/x:y` and reached the prerendered
  lookup, SvelteKit's router and `read()`, all of which decode before they
  open anything. The predicate (`utils/windows-path.js`) now decodes once
  when the path carries a `%` and refuses on either spelling; a path that does
  not decode is left to the lanes that refuse it themselves. Pure and pinned
  on every platform, and driven against the built runtime on Windows.
- **The liveness and readiness probes answer HEAD.** `healthCheckPath` and
  `readinessCheckPath` were registered for GET only, so a HEAD probe - the
  default for HAProxy's `httpchk` and for most uptime monitors - fell through
  to the catch-all and was answered by the app's own 404, which a balancer
  reads as an unhealthy instance. Both routes now register HEAD beside GET and
  answer it with the GET status, the body's length and no body;
  `createTestServer` registers the same pair. Pinned over a raw socket against
  the built runtime and through `fetch` against the test server.
- **The test server's admin lane refuses the fetch-forbidden methods the way
  production does.** `createTestServer` builds a `Request` for its admin route
  exactly as `handler/admin.js` does, and the same `TypeError` for `TRACE`,
  `TRACK` and `CONNECT` was caught by its construction guard and answered as a
  400 with a JSON body. The lane now checks `FORBIDDEN_METHODS` before anything
  else and answers through the shared `send405`, so the status, the `Allow`
  header and the body are the production ones and the `admin` handler is never
  called. Pinned over a raw socket against the published test server, beside
  the built-runtime case, since a fetch client refuses to send those methods.
- **A worker's uncaught exception no longer takes the whole process with it.**
  A worker thread holds uWS socket handles that libuv knows about and Node does
  not, so when Node tore the thread down after an uncaught exception the loop
  was closed with a poll handle still active and the process aborted:
  `uv_loop_close() while having open handles`. The restart supervisor never got
  to replace the worker, because the process it runs in was gone. The two other
  ways out of a worker - a graceful shutdown and a hard-tier assertion - already
  closed the App first for exactly this reason; the crash path did not.
  It does now, through the same clean exit: report the error to the primary,
  close the App so uWS releases its handles, let one loop turn run, then exit
  the worker. The primary emits the same `cluster.worker-error` event it emitted
  before, so an operator's timeline does not change - only the outcome does,
  from one aborted deployment to one replaced worker.
  An application that installs its own `uncaughtException` handler is untouched.
  Node keeps a worker alive when anything is listening, and an application that
  listens has taken responsibility for the exception, so the runtime defers
  whenever it is not the only listener rather than exiting underneath it.

- **The posture export describes the deployment when `workers` is set.** It is
  one socket path and the option is a build-time constant, so every worker
  evaluated the same install: each unlinked the previous owner's socket and
  bound its own, leaving only the last to bind reachable while the rest
  listened on orphaned inodes, and the first worker to shut down removed
  whichever socket was live at that moment. A consumer read one
  bind-order-chosen thread's posture and believed it was the server's - worse
  than reading none, since the export exists so an edge-defense daemon can act
  on it, and it would have acted on a quiet worker while a sibling was under
  siege.
  The primary owns the socket now. Each worker reports its posture inward on
  the same two occasions it used to push locally - every transition and every
  1 Hz sample - and the primary serves the aggregate: the highest posture any
  worker is in, carrying THAT worker's own `reason` and pressure numbers so
  the line stays internally consistent, plus a `workers` count of the threads
  it summarizes. The kernel readings are host-wide, so which worker they come
  from does not change them. A worker that exits is dropped rather than
  remembered - the aggregate is the worst worker, and a thread that died in
  siege would otherwise pin the deployment there for as long as the primary
  ran. The 1 Hz cadence is driven by the primary at a fixed rate rather than
  by the workers' samples, which would have made it a function of the worker
  count; when no worker has reported, the cadence stops, which is what the
  contract already means by silence. Single-process deployments are untouched:
  the worker still binds its own socket and its line carries no `workers`
  field. The path travels to the primary with the first report rather than
  through the environment, so the option stays the one place it is configured.

- **A publish can no longer claim to be a relayed frame.** `publishWire` has an
  origin side and a relay receive side, and one boolean picks between them: the
  relay side skips the clustered sequence-authority rule, skips the seq value
  check, skips the egress decision, skips the publish counter and the max-seen
  record, stamps the number it was handed instead of drawing the topic counter,
  and does not relay onward. All of that is correct for a frame a sibling
  worker already published and fanned out.
  That boolean was read from `_isRelay` and `_relaySeq` on the caller's options
  object - the same object every documented publish option arrives on - so an
  application could set them and be handled as the relay. It could then put an
  arbitrary number on a topic's sequence, off the publish ledger, past an armed
  egress ceiling, and out through the multi-origin relay the authority rule
  exists to keep unallocated numbers out of. Nothing refused it, and the
  hardening the same entry point already does against adversarial options
  objects sat one line above two keys anyone could type.
  The marker is not a key on that object any more. It is an argument compared
  by identity against a token the runtime never hands out, so no property
  lookup on caller-supplied data is left to satisfy. The relay decision reads
  the same token instead of a `relay: false` the internal caller had to pass
  beside it, so the two settings can no longer disagree. The batch surfaces
  needed nothing: their options copy is field reads rather than a spread, so
  the keys never reached the entries. `test/relay-marker-real.test.js` drives
  the built runtime and asserts the seq the client receives, which is the
  observable projection of that one boolean.

- **A marker on a caller's options object is compared by identity, not
  truthiness.** Naming an internal marker with a `Symbol` keeps a caller from
  spelling it, which is not the same as keeping them from answering it: a
  caller never has to name a key, only to pass an object that answers for every
  key. `new Proxy({}, { get: () => true })`, or an ordinary getter inherited
  from a prototype, satisfies any property-shaped marker without knowing what
  it is called. That let `platform.publish(topic, event, data, forged)` skip the
  admission decision and publish straight past a crossed egress ceiling.
  The batch-admission marker still rides the options object, because the batch
  lanes copy those objects per entry, but neither its key nor its VALUE leaves
  the module that owns them and every lane writes and reads it through one
  pair of helpers. The value is a second symbol that is never used as a key,
  which is what a `get` trap cannot answer: such a trap is handed the key it is
  asked for, so a marker whose value is its own key is echoed straight back.
  The write defines the property rather than assigning it, because a plain
  assignment walks the prototype chain: an accessor installed for that key on
  `Object.prototype` both receives the token and stops the own property being
  created. That second half needed no attacker - any application with an
  accessor on that key made every batch entry re-decide, so a batch delivered a
  prefix and dropped its tail.
  `createTestServer` and the dev plugin take the same decision. The forgery
  case that already existed listed five spellings of the key; it now also
  carries the shapes that name nothing, including the echo.

- **A worker that reports ready and never attaches its relay reader is now
  detected.** The primary hands a worker no relay frames until it reports its
  reader live, which is what keeps a slow boot out of the spill ceiling's reach
  - the ceiling is a stall detector, and a booting worker's unread ring looks
  exactly like a stall. The cost of that gate was the detection that used to
  come with it: a worker that reported ready and then never attached received
  no frames, so no spill accumulated, nothing crossed the age ceiling, and it
  kept acking heartbeats while missing every cross-worker publish its own
  subscribers were owed. The boot deadline could not catch it either, because
  that deadline only applies while a worker is not yet ready.
  The primary now stamps when a worker reported ready and escalates one that
  has not attached within the steady heartbeat timeout, through the same
  request-exit and respawn path as an unresponsive worker. A healthy worker
  attaches in the same tick it goes ready - the two are posted synchronously
  one after the other - so the bound is enormously generous and needs no
  configuration. It is deliberately not tied to `WORKER_BOOT_TIMEOUT_MS`:
  setting that to `0` says an init may take arbitrarily long, which is a
  different statement from allowing a serving worker to miss relay traffic
  forever.

- **The restart budget is stamped on the attach, not on ready.** The attach
  regime above kills only after the steady window, and
  the supervisor's stable window is the same length, so a worker stamped at
  `ready` would read as stably up at every such kill, reset its attempts, and
  a deterministic attach failure would restart once per window for as long as
  the process lived. Stamped on the attach, each kill is one more attempt
  against the slot and the failure walks to `ADAPTER-ERR-WORKER-RESTART-LIMIT`
  like any other crash loop. A healthy worker attaches in the tick after it
  goes ready, so the stamp moves by one tick and nothing else changes for it.

- **`vite dev` applies custom 101 response headers instead of warning that it
  cannot.** `upgradeResponse(userData, headers)` put application headers on the
  handshake in production and dropped them in development, with a warning
  saying the `ws` library does not support custom 101 headers. That reason was
  wrong: `ws` assembles the handshake response itself and emits the assembled
  header lines for inspection before writing them, which is all this needs. An
  app that set a header on connect could not see it work until it deployed.
  Dev now appends the validated headers to that response, so the same handshake
  goes out in both places. The array form stays several headers of one name
  rather than a comma-joined value, which is what multiple `Set-Cookie`
  requires. Validation is unchanged and still runs first, so a malformed name
  or value is refused in development exactly as production refuses it - the
  point of validating in dev at all is that a broken upgrade cannot pass there
  and fail only in production. The `Set-Cookie` advisory now comes from the
  same shared helper production uses, so the two cannot drift.

- **A connection's own state can no longer be silenced from the prototype
  chain.** The runtime keeps per-connection state on the socket's `userData`
  object under `Symbol.for` keys, written with plain assignments. A plain
  assignment is a `[[Set]]`: it walks the prototype chain, and the object uWS
  hands to `open` inherits from `uWS.WebSocket`, whose chain reaches
  `Object.prototype`. An accessor installed there for one of those keys
  received the value and left no own property behind, so the write did nothing
  at all. The keys are reachable by design - `Symbol.for` is what lets a
  bundled copy of a module and a runtime-loaded one resolve the same slot - so
  this needed no hostile code, only an application with an accessor on the key.
  Losing the value was the smaller half. Every one of those sites is a lazy
  initialization or a transition behind a falsy guard, so a swallowed write
  left the guard open and its lane re-ran the initialization on every pass: the
  subscription set rebuilt empty, the coalesce buffer reallocated per message
  and coalescing nothing, the wire-id space restarting.
  `open` now declares every slot as an own property before anything writes one,
  so each later assignment finds an own property and never consults the chain
  again. A slot that is already populated is left untouched, because that is
  the evidence `ws.platform-double-init` reads to refuse a re-entrant open. The
  declaration cannot ride the upgrade object instead: uWS copies that object
  into its own with `[[Set]]`, so a slot declared there is intercepted on the
  way across and arrives absent. Slot presence is no longer a signal that a
  lane has allocated anything; the value is.

- **The process-wide slots are defined the same way.** The slots that have no
  connection to hang a declaration on live on `globalThis` under `Symbol.for`
  keys, so one accessor on `Object.prototype` takes the publication for every
  copy of the module at once, and each is written once per process - exactly
  the write an accessor meets. The operational event sink and its registry, the
  ingress kind registry, the derived and plugin-owned topic prefixes, the
  side-effect hook marker, the shared-cohort hooks, the subscription accounting
  sink, the settled-registry set, the dev dashboard's contributor map and the
  dropped-field warning set are all defined rather than assigned.
  `test/connection-slot-declaration.test.js` installs the accessor first and
  then uses each process-wide slot through its public entry point, so a write
  that reached the accessor fails the case.

- **The admin route's matched path and its reported path are now the same
  path.** The route is registered on the raw prefix and uWS matches the raw
  request target, but constructing a Web `Request` resolves dot segments. So
  `GET /__realtime/../reflect` matched `/__realtime/*`, reached
  `handleAdminRequest`, and handed the app's `admin(request)` a request whose
  pathname was `/reflect`; two segments up reached it as `/escape`. Every
  dispatch and authorization decision such a handler makes reads that pathname,
  so it was deciding about a path the router had never matched.
  The URL is now parsed once, before any body is read, and a request whose
  resolved pathname has left the prefix is answered 400 - not rewritten, since
  a target whose route and whose self-description disagree is ambiguous, and
  silently picking either reading would let a caller aim the admin lane at a
  path of their choosing. Normalization itself is not the fault:
  `/__realtime/a/../introspect` resolves back inside and is served, with the
  resolved path reported. A percent-encoded `..%2f` is one opaque segment
  rather than a dot segment, so it keeps the prefix and is served too. The
  parsed URL is reused to build the `Request`, so the check costs no extra
  allocation on a route that is cold by construction.
  The prefix now has ONE derivation, exported from `handler/config.js` beside
  the other options-derived constants and read by both the route registration
  and the check - two derivations of one prefix is one edit away from a check
  that describes a different route than the one that matched. `createTestServer`
  takes the same decision. `test/admin-path-confusion-real.test.js` drives the
  built runtime over RAW SOCKETS, because every HTTP client resolves the target
  before sending it: `fetch('/__realtime/../reflect')` puts `/reflect` on the
  wire, never reaches the route, and would pass against the defect.

- **`protection: 'auto'` is not inert without an admission ceiling.** The
  declaration said it was. Escalation from `'normal'` to `'elevated'` counts
  consecutive active pressure samples and reads nothing from the admission
  gate, and `startPressureSampling` runs unconditionally wherever the WebSocket
  endpoint is registered - so an app that sets `protection: 'auto'` and no
  ceiling does reach elevated, where every refusal widens its `Retry-After`
  jitter. What actually needs a ceiling is the step INTO `'siege'`: its
  threshold is the ceiling's admit rate doubled, and with no ceiling the gate
  emits no capacity reject and the threshold is `Infinity`. A pinned level is
  not a resolution at all and needs nothing from the gate.
  No behaviour changed here - the declaration did. The configuration the
  sentence described was the one configuration nothing in the suite drove:
  every posture case handed the machine a gate, which is how the claim
  survived. `test/protection-posture-unit.test.js` now drives it with no
  admission at all, in both directions - elevated is reached, siege stays
  unreachable however long the pressure lasts.

- **The batch pre-passes vet seq VALUES, not just the deployment shape.**
  `batch()` and `publishBatched()` both open with an atomic pre-pass whose
  stated purpose is to refuse the whole call before any part of it is
  published. Both asked `assertClusterSequenceAuthority`, which is a TOPOLOGY
  question - and `clusterSequenceValuesAccepted` returns accepted immediately
  when the runtime is not multi-worker, without reading the value. So on the
  default single-worker deployment the pre-pass vetted nothing a caller had
  written, and message k's bad `seq` surfaced later, differently on each
  surface. `batch()` threw from inside `platform.publish` with messages 0..k-1
  already fanned out - the published prefix its own comment says must not
  happen. `publishBatched()` threw from its stamping loop, which delivers
  nothing (the send is at the end) but has already ADVANCED THE TOPIC COUNTER
  and written the max-seen map for every earlier entry: the counter then skips
  numbers no client ever saw, so a watermark can sit above a value that was
  never sent and a republish of it after the payload is fixed reads as
  already-seen, with nothing on the wire to notice by.

- **Both batch pre-passes now ask the value question themselves.** Each calls
  `assertStampableSeq` on the value it has already snapshotted, independent of
  topology, before the first publish and before the first stamp.
  `publishWireBatch` was already right - it validates every entry in its
  snapshot pass - and `vite dev` needs nothing, because it stamps no seq and so
  has no mid-batch throw to hoist. `src/testing.js` takes the same order on
  both surfaces, since an application certifying against `createTestServer` has
  to see the atomicity it will get in production.
  `test/batch-seq-atomic-real.test.js` drives the built runtime. Its
  `publishBatched` case advertises the `batch` capability deliberately: without
  it the call degrades to the per-event loop and the stamping loop under test
  never runs. That case asserts the COUNTER rather than delivery, because that
  lane delivers nothing either way - the counter is the only thing that can
  carry the claim, and the two topics it uses are kept separate so the expected
  first value stays exactly 1.

- **A seq refusal no longer waits for the egress ceiling to relax.** The
  publish lanes validated a `seq` as a side effect of stamping it, and the
  stamp is the last step they take: the ceiling decides first. So with a
  budget armed and its window crossed, `publish(topic, event, data, { seq:
  '5' })` returned `false` - which is also the ordinary answer under load,
  carries no signal that anything is wrong, and is what a caller's retry logic
  is written around. The `TypeError` arrived only once traffic dropped,
  pointing at a deploy that could be weeks old. `assertStampableSeq` now asks
  the value question ahead of the admission decision in `publish` and
  `publishWire`, and inside the batch call gate for `publishWireBatch` - which
  also moves that surface's refusal ahead of the empty-batch early return, so
  an empty call refuses what a full one refuses rather than answering `false`
  for a value it would throw on the moment one entry is added. The harness's
  `publish` takes the same order, so an application certifying against
  `createTestServer` meets the error it will meet in production.
  The check delegates to `stampSeqValue` rather than restating its table, and
  returns early for the two counter spellings - the only arms that read a
  counter map - so it can be handed none at all: a delegation that ever fell
  through to the counter dereferences the absent map and its verdict stops
  matching the stamp's, which `test/seq-stamp.test.js` compares value by
  value, message included. `test/publish-seq-refusal-order-real.test.js`
  drives the built runtime with the ceiling proven to be shedding first, so a
  run where the budget never armed cannot report the claim as verified.

- **`staticHeaders` refuses a name or value that could split a response.**
  `normalizeStaticHeaders` validated the value's TYPE and nothing else, so a
  configured string carrying CR, LF or NUL passed the build and reached
  `res.writeHeader` verbatim. Those bytes terminate a header field on the
  wire, so the remainder of the value is written as further headers - or,
  after a blank line, as a second response body. The value is now scanned for
  all three, and the NAME is held to the RFC 9110 token grammar rather than
  scanned for the same bytes: anything outside `1*tchar` cannot appear in a
  legal field name anyway, and an allowlist cannot be outflanked the way a
  denylist can. Both predicates are the handshake lane's, imported rather than
  restated: a narrower class was tried there once and reverted for letting VT,
  FF and DEL onto the wire, and a fifth private copy of the same rule is the
  drift that module exists to end. Validation runs BEFORE the reserved-key
  drop, so a reserved name is reported rather than silently discarded, and the
  name is checked before lowercasing - some non-ASCII letters fold INTO the
  token alphabet.
  Refused at build rather than sanitised per request, because rewriting a
  configured value at send time leaves an operator believing the header they
  wrote is the header being served. `test/static-headers.test.js` drives the
  splitting payloads, the illegal names, the legal punctuation set, and the
  ordering against the reserved drop.

- **The cursor plugin reads the envelope the runtime already parsed.** The
  adapter decodes and parses a small JSON object frame once and hands it to
  every hook as `MessageContext.msg`, which the type documents as the way to
  avoid "re-running `TextDecoder + JSON.parse` on every frame". The cursor
  hook ignored it and re-did both, allocating a `TextDecoder` per message, on
  a hook that inspects every frame rather than only cursor frames. It now
  takes `msg` when present and falls back to a process-wide decoder for the
  shapes the type documents as absent - binary, over 8 KiB, not a plain
  object. The fallback also stops reading `.type` off a value that parsed to
  `null`: `JSON.parse('null')` succeeds and those reads sit outside the catch,
  so the frame `null` raised `TypeError` out of the hook. Measured against an
  identical control arm at a 1.5% noise floor: 422 ns/frame before, 2.8 ns
  after, with the decoder allocation 99 ns of the difference.
  `test/cursor.test.js` makes the pre-parsed envelope and the raw bytes name
  different topics, so which one the hook acted on is observable.

- **A ref-less recover subscribe answers with an uncorrelatable error.** The
  family ack policy is deliberate silence for a subscribe without a `ref` -
  the client said it would not listen - but the recover lane is the one
  request whose reply the client must correlate: a caller replaying an offset
  that the saturated pending-subscribe gate (or any silent denial) swallowed
  believed itself subscribed and resumed into a silent gap. A subscribe
  carrying `recover` where a resume hook exists is now refused up front, when
  no `ref` rides it, with `{"type":"error","code":"RECOVER_REQUIRES_REF",
  "topic":...}` - the established shape for frames that answer for no
  correlatable request - and a `subscribe-batch` whose recover map names any
  history refuses whole with `topic: null`, before any entry is inspected.
  One shared predicate and frame builder serve production, `createTestServer`
  and the Vite dev plugin, so the surfaces cannot drift; plain ref-less
  subscribes keep their silence, and `recover` with no resume hook stays
  ignored. The code is registered in PROTOCOL.md, in section 3.7 beside
  `CONTROL_FRAME_TOO_LARGE` and in the C.4 registry, and section 3.2's
  silent-mode rule carries the carve-out: an unregistered code is one a
  conforming client is required to IGNORE, so the refusal would have been
  dropped by exactly the hand-rolled clients it exists for.
  `test/recover-ref-contract.test.js` holds the refusal, the with-ref control,
  and both preserved silences on all three surfaces;
  `test/protocol-schema.test.js` pins every emitted error code against the
  registry in both directions.

- **A batch call-level `excludeWs` is the default exclusion for every entry.**
  `publishWireBatch` forwarded its options to the per-entry path on the
  stateless lane - where `excludeWs` rode along as an undocumented side
  effect - and derived exclusions from the entries alone on the stateful
  lane. Which lane runs is a property of the codec (`state` opts into batch
  framing), so the documented way to adopt batch framing silently dropped a
  working call's exclusion: the author-echo bug. The call-level socket now
  defaults every entry on both lanes, and an entry's own `excludeWs`
  overrides it - the same override shape the entry `seq` takes; an entry
  `null` means absent (inherit) on both lanes, where the stateless lane
  previously read it as an override to nothing. Egress delivery deductions
  ride the same per-entry resolution, so the ledger counts what actually
  fanned out. `test/publish-batch-exclude-real.test.js` reads the contract
  off frames two real clients receive, on both lanes.

- **The relay fan-out skips a worker until its reader is live.** The primary
  forwarded relay frames into a worker's ring from the moment of spawn, but
  the worker drains only after module evaluation, its init hook and warmup -
  so the age ceiling, measured from the spill's birth, judged a booting
  worker by the steady-state stall detector: under sustained relay traffic
  the fresh ring filled, the 5s ceiling quarantined the still-booting
  worker, and its respawn landed in the same window, converting one crash at
  relay peak into restart-limit exhaustion and a whole-process exit (the
  stable-uptime budget reset never applied because the slot never stayed
  ready). A worker now reports its relay reader live and the fan-out skips
  it until then, so the ring of a booting worker stays empty and there is no
  backlog to misjudge - for a boot of any duration, which no second deadline
  inside the writer could have covered, since the writer cannot tell a slow
  boot from a dead one. Nothing is owed to that worker yet either: it
  already treats everything from before that moment as a stream it joined
  mid-flight. The three sites that consult the age ceiling now share one
  decision rather than repeating the comparison - the flush wake, which the
  consumer's own drain triggers, was the one that had drifted.
  `test/relay-ring.test.js` pins the shared decision, the re-dating on drain
  progress, and the unchanged quarantine for a drained-then-stalled
  consumer; `test/cluster-relay-attach-gate.test.js` pins the gate.

- **The relay frame ceiling measures the unit its neighbors measure.** The
  sender-side admission compared `String.prototype.length` - UTF-16 code
  units - while the per-peer spill ceilings and the reader's reassembly cap
  count encoded bytes. A ceiling-sized multibyte envelope (up to three bytes
  per code unit) passed admission, fit the reader's headroom, and landed over
  `CLUSTER_RELAY_MAX_PENDING_KB` in every receiver's backlog at once when the
  ring was behind - one publish quarantining every healthy sibling, which is
  the exact failure the ceiling split was built to prevent. Admission now
  decides on `Buffer.byteLength`, with the free length read kept as the fast
  path: UTF-8 never encodes below one byte or above three per code unit, so
  only an envelope inside that band walks the string, once. The batched lane
  sums the same way and still refuses wholesale. Refusals report the exact
  encoded size. `test/relay-frame-ceiling.test.js` holds the three-byte and
  astral refusals on both lanes, the band admit, the summed batch refusal,
  and admission at exactly the ceiling.

- **The consistency auditor stops fabricating `subs.total-mismatch` from its
  own skipped reads.** `buildConnectionAuditSnapshot` attached the cap
  accountant whenever the caller asked for the whole range (`offset === 0 &&
  total <= limit`), but a connection whose `getUserData` throws is skipped
  inside that walk, and its close has not run, so the counter still holds its
  memberships. The window came back one connection short while the counter was
  complete, and `checkTotalSubscriptions` reported the difference as drift. The
  condition is now `out.length === total` - what the cross-check actually
  needs, and one test in place of the two cases anyone thought to name: an
  offset, a limit below the population, and a skipped handle all fail it
  together. A complete window is unchanged and still runs every predicate, and
  a real drift still reports. `test/auditor-snapshot.test.js` drives the freed
  handle through the builder and asserts the predicate stays silent, then holds
  the other side so the guard cannot degrade into disabling the accountant.

- **The reserved admin prefix now holds against a target that arrives inside
  it.** uWS matches the mount against the raw request target, while every lane
  behind it reads a different spelling of that target: the SSR `Request`
  resolves the path, and both the prerendered lookup and SvelteKit's router
  percent-decode before matching. So two shapes missed the mount and reached
  the app's own routing inside the namespace the adapter documents as reserved
  and mounts ahead of page routing - `/foo/../__realtime/introspect`, where
  resolution drops a segment, and `/%5f%5frealtime/introspect`, where decoding
  spells the prefix and no dot segment is involved at all. Which happened was
  the caller's spelling to choose.
  The mirror of the escape the admin lane already refuses, and refused the same
  way: the main request edge answers 400 when a target arrives in the prefix its
  raw form was outside of. Not rerouted into the admin lane - that picks one of
  the two readings on the caller's behalf, and would let a caller reach that
  lane through a spelling a fronting proxy's ACL does not read as admin.

- **What bounds that check.** It runs only while the route is mounted, since the
  mount is what reserves the prefix; with no `admin` export both spellings reach
  the app anyway and refusing one would take away a path the app serves. The
  namespace test is the mount's own - `/__realtime/` and below, leaving the bare
  prefix on the catch-all where uWS leaves it. It sits AHEAD of the prerendered
  lookup, which decodes too, so a prerendered page inside the prefix cannot
  answer the encoded spelling first; the static fast path needs no such care,
  matching raw pathnames against built asset keys that no encoded spelling hits.
  The decode is `decodeURIComponent`, stronger than the router's, because the
  two lanes below disagree about `%2F` and the stronger reading covers both.
  A one-pass character scan decides the rest for free: a path can arrive in the
  prefix only by DROPPING a segment - a dot segment (`.` or `%2e`), a backslash,
  or the whitespace the URL parser strips - or by SPELLING one of the prefix's
  own characters encoded (`%`), so a path carrying none of the five never
  reaches the resolution. That scan measures 7.8 ns per request and the resolve
  408 ns on the paths that take it.
  `test/admin-prefix-entry-real.test.js` drives the resolved and encoded
  spellings over raw sockets, because every HTTP client resolves the target
  before sending it, and the fixture app carries a real route inside the prefix
  so a failure is the app answering a reserved path rather than a status code
  standing in for one. It also prerenders a page there, which is what makes the
  ordering testable rather than assumed.
  `test/admin-prefix-unmounted-real.test.js` holds the other side: with no admin
  handler the same targets are served by that route and that page - which is
  also what proves the prerendered entry exists, since the mount shadows every
  spelling that reaches it.

- **A closing socket leaves the live set first.** The close finally released
  the permit, the subscription accounting, the capability counts, the wire
  states, the shared wire-id refs and the send-gate slot, and the removal
  from `wsConnections` sat last. None of those releases is individually
  guarded, so one throw skipped everything after it - including the removal.
  A stranded entry does not sit still: every publish walk keeps visiting a
  socket whose handle is gone, and its registry keeps counting toward the
  auditor's summed bookkeeping while the accountant has already released
  those memberships, which reads as a ledger mismatch no double charge
  explains and which never clears. The removal owes nothing to the releases
  below it, so it goes first. `test/close-path-ordering.test.js` pins the
  order in the close handler itself - the removal is its own statement, it
  precedes every release that can throw, and it appears exactly once - because
  what has to hold is the position, and a runtime case can only reach the
  arrangement through whichever release it chose to break.

- **The relay ring reads a frame length as unsigned.** `|` yields a signed
  32-bit result, so a prefix with bit 31 set decoded negative - and a
  negative length walks past every guard: it is not greater than the ceiling,
  so the oversized refusal is skipped; it is not greater than the bytes on
  hand, so the wait-for-more break never fires; and `offset += 4 + len`
  drives the parse offset deeply negative, after which the loop emits empty
  frames four bytes at a time until it climbs back to zero. So a corrupt or
  hostile prefix wedged the reader thread that the ceiling exists to protect,
  from exactly the input class its own comment claims to handle. Read
  unsigned, the same bytes are an enormous frame, which is what they claim to
  be and what the ceiling already refuses. The case in
  `test/relay-ring.test.js` closes the reader from its frame callback, so the
  pre-fix arithmetic fails it in milliseconds rather than spinning half a
  billion iterations inside the suite.

- **`If-Range` is evaluated with the strong comparison.** Every validator this
  lane issues is weak by construction - mtime and size, spelled `W/"..."` -
  and the range gate accepted one as an `If-Range` match. RFC 9110 s13.1.5
  requires the strong comparison there, and a weak validator never
  strong-matches. It is not pedantry: `If-Range` exists so a client can splice
  a slice onto bytes it already holds, and a weak validator does not promise
  those bytes are the same octets - two representations that differ may share
  one. Splicing across that yields a corrupt body under a 206 saying it is
  fine. A weak `If-Range` now falls through to the full representation, which
  is the fallback a malformed or multi-range header already takes. A plain
  `Range` is untouched: it claims no consistency, and it is what a resuming
  download manager sends, which is why this costs almost nothing in practice.
  Two cases in `test/static-assets-negotiate.test.js` changed with it - both
  asserted that a matching tag resumes, which is the behaviour being removed -
  and they now pin the refusal and the plain-`Range` resume separately, so
  selecting a representation and being allowed to splice it are tested as the
  different questions they are.

- **A resume frame's epoch map takes the observer gate.** The frame carries two
  client-named maps: `lastSeenSeqs` went through the gate and had its
  ungranted topics dropped, while `lastSeenEpochs` was handed to the hook
  exactly as parsed. They arrive on one frame, keyed the same way, and the
  hook reads them together - checking for an epoch mismatch means iterating
  the epoch map. So the gate dropped a topic from one hand and returned it
  with the other, carrying its generation as well as its name. Both maps now
  take one filter, written once so they cannot drift. The fixture echoes the
  epoch keys the hook received, which is what makes the drop observable;
  asserting on absent replay traffic would pass against a server with no
  resume hook at all. Removing the epoch filter fails the case in
  `test/resume-grant-gate-real.test.js` with the ungranted topic in the list.

- **`PORT=0` is refused under reuseport.** Under reuseport every I/O worker
  calls `listen()` for itself, so an ephemeral port hands each of them a
  different one and the single shared port reuseport exists to provide never
  happens. The fleet boots green and serves where nothing routes: the
  balancer, the health check and the startup log all name port 0. Acceptor
  mode is untouched and must be - the primary binds once and hands
  descriptors to the workers, so one ephemeral port is still one port; that
  is the control case. Refused as `ADAPTER-ERR-CLUSTER-CONFIG-PORT` with the
  other capacity misconfigurations, before any worker spawns. The cases in
  `test/error-registry-cluster-config.test.js` are Linux-only, and not
  because the refusal is: off Linux reuseport is already refused by its own
  id, which fires first, so the condition cannot be reached there and a case
  that ran would assert the wrong refusal.

- **The certificate watcher listens for its own error event.** A watch fails
  two ways. Failing to START throws, and both callers already wrap `start()`
  to degrade instead of crashing. Failing AFTER it started - a permission
  change, the platform's watch resources exhausted - arrives as an `error`
  EVENT when the platform reports it at all, and no one was listening; an
  `error` event with no listener is rethrown by EventEmitter, so a certificate
  watcher could raise an uncaught exception on a process that was serving
  fine, and on a cluster primary that ends the whole fleet.
  The listener is attached whether or not the caller passes `onError`, because
  not crashing is the point and being told is the option. A watch that has died
  is not re-armed by anything, so it is closed rather than left to fire again,
  a pending debounce is dropped rather than fired into a directory the watch
  just lost, and a late error from a watcher `stop()` already replaced is
  ignored. Reported as `ADAPTER-ERR-TLS-WATCH-LOST`, or
  `ADAPTER-ERR-TLS-PRIMARY-WATCH-LOST` on the primary - their own ids rather
  than the existing watch ids, whose text promises a failure at start and an
  arm-time catch-up read that this case does not get.
  `test/tls-reload.test.js` drives the event through the injected `watchFs`
  seam, and pins the EventEmitter contract the whole thing rests on against a
  BARE emitter, so that assertion cannot pass because of the code it justifies.

- **A watched certificate directory that is removed or replaced ends the
  watch, and a moved one where the platform says so.** No platform reports
  that through `error`. Measured: on Windows
  a removed directory makes the watcher narrate its own deletion at about a
  hundred thousand `rename` events a second for as long as the process runs
  and never raises `error`, and the events keep coming after a new directory
  is created at the same path - the handle is on the deleted one. So a removed
  certificate directory was a permanent timer churn, a failing read and a log
  line every debounce window and, on a cluster primary, a reload broadcast to
  every worker on the same cadence. On Linux the same removal delivers one
  `rename` for the directory itself and then nothing, the recreated directory
  is a new inode inotify never watched, and `watching` stayed `true` for a
  watch that would never see another renewal.

- **How the watcher now tells a dead directory from a live one.**
  What both platforms DO deliver is an event that names the watched directory
  rather than an entry inside it - inotify spells it as the directory's
  basename, Windows as its full path - and that spelling is what the watcher
  now acts on: it stats the directory and compares the inode identity recorded
  at start. Gone, or a different inode at the same path, is a dead watch,
  closed and reported through the same lost-watch ids and the same sticky
  degraded state as a platform-reported death. A replaced directory gets one
  final debounced read first, because what replaced it is very often the
  renewal, and on the primary that reload is broadcast. An event that names an
  entry never stats, so a renewal burst costs nothing new, and the same
  spelling on a live directory - a `chmod`, a subdirectory appearing - keeps
  its inode and reloads as before. Nothing detects a directory moved aside on
  Windows: that produces no event at all.
  `test/tls-reload.test.js` drives every branch through the injected `watchFs`
  and `statFs` seams, and two cases remove and rebuild a real directory under
  a real `fs.watch` so the spelling the seams assume is the one the platform
  sends; both are mutation-checked.

- **The cluster primary reads its TLS degraded-state policy from the ledger.**
  Which degradations a success can clear is policy, and the primary carried a
  second copy of it inline: a clear that ended the degradation on any successful
  read, with no equivalent of the sticky watch reason the worker half keeps. Now
  both halves answer through `createTlsDegradedLedger`, so a dead watch stays
  degraded through any later success on either side.
  On the primary that success is reachable: a certificate directory replaced
  by a new one at the same path ends the watch and is then read once more,
  and when the replacement reads cleanly that read is a success following a
  watch death. The inline clear would have ended the degradation there, on a
  process that will never see the next renewal. The case drives the real
  watcher and the real ledger composed the way the primary composes them and
  holds the degradation through the final read; the primary also keeps its
  watcher reference after the report, because the final read's timer is the
  watcher's and only `stop()` at shutdown clears it.

- **The dedup leader decides sharing before it holds the body.** The leader
  path did `await response.arrayBuffer()` and compared the result with
  `MAX_SSR_DEDUP_BODY` afterwards, so the cap bounded what was SHARED and
  nothing bounded what was HELD: every uncredentialed GET or HEAD that reached
  the branch materialised its whole body per request before a byte was
  written, which is exactly what a public media route serves to a first-time
  visitor. Two pieces replace it in `ssr-dedup.js`: `declaresBodyPastCap`
  sends a response whose `Content-Length` is past the cap straight to the
  streaming write, and `readBodyUpTo` reads an undeclared body only until it
  ends or its bytes pass the cap, handing back either the whole body (shared
  as before) or a stream that replays the chunks already read and then
  continues from the source, released as they replay. A leader that passes
  the cap therefore streams the body it will not share, and a waiter that
  attached to it falls through to its own render as it always did. Held by a
  fixture route that emits its first chunk at once and the rest after a
  pause: the first bytes of a body past the cap arrive during the pause
  (buffering would deliver nothing until after it), two concurrent anonymous
  requests for it both complete and both render, and two for a body within
  the cap still render once.

- **The streamed write holds under backpressure on the pinned build.** The
  chunk writer parks on a drain promise when `res.write` reports backpressure
  and the socket's writable event wakes it. Measured in a Linux container with
  the TCP buffers shrunk so a pausing client drives real backpressure: under
  the addon build the 0.5.x line pins (v20.67.0, native uWS v20.77.0) the
  writable wakeup is lost after the first or second backpressure event, the
  writer waits out its 30 s deadline and closes the socket on a body cut at
  180 to 260 KB of 1 MiB; under the pinned v20.69.0 (native v20.79.0) the
  same loop delivers 2 MiB and 4 MiB bodies through thirty to sixty
  backpressure events, over plain HTTP and TLS. Draining the socket from
  inside the handler does not rescue the older build either, so the fix is
  the pin and nothing on the write path changes. Backpressure is a
  socket-buffer event, not a client-speed one: on a real link a body a few
  hundred kilobytes long produces it at gigabit speeds, and the field report
  saw the cut with a fast client; loopback needs a pausing reader only
  because its buffers hold megabytes. The suite therefore streams 16 MiB to a
  client that pauses after every read, over plain HTTP and TLS, and requires
  the terminating chunk: a build that loses the wakeup fails it on the byte
  count after the deadline instead of hanging.

- **The handshake's own header names are not the application's to write.**
  `findUnsafeUpgradeHeader` said which BYTES a 101 header may carry and
  which names are tokens, and nothing said which names the handshake owns.
  uWS appends its own `Connection`, `Upgrade` and `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`
  after the application's headers, and `ws` assembles its own first, so an
  application value for one of those went out as a second line of the same
  name; a forged `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` produced a 101 carrying two, which a
  conforming client refuses. Low severity - the bag is application-authored
  and the client fails closed - but a shared gap the shared predicate was
  built to close. It now refuses those three plus `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions`
  and `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, which the server negotiates from the client's
  offer, compared case-insensitively, with the same consequence as an unsafe
  byte: the helper throws, a duck-typed result takes the hook-error path, no
  partial 101. Six named shape vectors join the shared table, so all three
  surfaces are held to the refusal by the same cases, each reading the raw
  response for the marker the refused value carried.
  Measured while there: a value with a code unit in 0x80-0xFF leaves as the
  same two UTF-8 octets on every surface (uWS and `ws` both encode a JS
  string as UTF-8), so the range stays legal and the dev suite now pins the
  spelling the other two already did.

## [0.6.0-next.94] - 2026-08-26

<!-- consumer-release-summary:start -->
### Consumer summary

- **Changed: the topic epoch reports a per-topic generation after a confirmed relay loss.** Every topic previously shared the one per-process generation; a topic whose relayed history a worker proved it lost now carries a freshly minted value on that worker, so its subscribe acks and resume compares repudiate offsets taken before the loss.
  - **Affects:** Resume hooks and replay backends comparing `platform.topicEpoch(topic)`; the value is unchanged for every topic without a confirmed relay loss.
  - **Action:** None; hooks that compare for equality, as documented, inherit the behavior.
  - **Requires:** No new dependency or option.
  - **Compatibility:** The epoch stays an opaque equality-only integer of the same shape; only when it can change moved. Overrides are bounded (4096 topics, oldest-undisturbed evicted) and reset with the process.
  - **Detail:** [Changed engineering detail](#changed).
- **Fixed: a relay-gap resync now reaches subscribers that disconnected before the loss was confirmed.** The gap marker walks live connections, so a client that took the stepping sequences and dropped inside the confirmation grace kept a poisoned resume offset; a confirmed loss now mints the topic a new epoch, so that offset cold-rehydrates at its next resume.
  - **Affects:** Multi-worker deployments running the cross-worker state reporter, and clients that never negotiated `relay.resync:1` as well; a reconnect onto a sibling worker already mismatched that worker's own generation, so the mint closes the losing worker's one remaining lane.
  - **Action:** None; the epoch compare is machinery every client already implements, and the bundled client always presents its recorded epochs.
  - **Requires:** No new dependency or option.
  - **Compatibility:** No wire change. The mint is local to the losing worker, whose other resuming subscribers of the topic pay one cold re-snapshot; an offset presented without an epoch matches by the protocol's own rule and stays unrepaired.
  - **Detail:** [Fixed engineering detail](#fixed).

- **Fixed: one unreadable cgroup file could pin memory pressure to a looser wall.** A failed read of the nearest group's limit file, while a looser ancestor answered, latched that ancestor for the process life; the signal then measured against a far larger wall than the kernel kills on and stayed low into an out-of-memory death.
  - **Affects:** Containerized deployments whose cgroup hierarchy nests a tighter limit under a looser parent, where a limit file read can fail transiently.
  - **Action:** None.
  - **Requires:** No new dependency or option.
  - **Compatibility:** Discovery latches only after a clean probe; an incomplete sample reports the best wall it saw and retries next tick, so a healthy container behaves exactly as before and no threshold, option, or metric name moved.
  - **Detail:** [Fixed engineering detail](#fixed).

<!-- consumer-release-summary:end -->

### Changed

- **`platform.topicEpoch` consults a per-topic override map before the
  process generation.** `topicEpochValue` (utils/epoch.js) is the single read
  authority - the platform method, the subscribe ack (including its defensive
  fallback), and every resume compare route through it - so a minted value
  reaches each site at once. Overrides install through `overrideTopicEpoch`,
  bounded at 4096 entries with the longest-undisturbed entry evicted at the
  cap (an evicted topic falls back to the process generation, the honest
  degradation for a loss window old enough to outlive the cap).
  `test/topic-epoch.test.js` pins the fallback identity, the in-place
  replace, the recency eviction, and the harness reset.

### Fixed

- **A client's permit-starved backlog reaches the server while it is
  growing.** The bundled client asks for a replenish once per window, and the
  window empties before the queue fills - so the one frame the window allowed
  left with an empty queue, the once-per-window latch closed behind it, and
  every send that piled up afterwards was invisible. The `queued` field the
  server folds into its saturation reading therefore reported zero through
  exactly the episode it exists to measure, and only an undersized re-grant
  could produce a non-zero depth. The client now also reports on each
  DOUBLING of the backlog, independently of the prefetch latch: the server
  learns a starving connection is starving, while the control frames stay
  logarithmic in the queue bound - at most nine for a window that fills the
  whole 256-deep queue, and none at all for a connection that never starves.
  `test/lease-client.test.js` drives the default 256 window to exhaustion
  with no contrived re-grant and fails when the growth report is removed.

- **A respawned simulator worker presents a new topic generation.** The
  multi-worker simulator derived each worker's generation from its id, so a
  respawn handed the worker back the exact token it carried before - a
  restarted worker claiming continuity with a sequence space it had just
  reset. Production cannot do this: every worker latches its own random token
  and a restart re-latches, which is what makes a client's held offset die
  against the restarted worker and forces the cold re-read. The sim now
  counts worker incarnations in creation order, so every worker and every
  respawn of one presents a distinct token that still reproduces across runs.
  The initial cohort's tokens are unchanged by construction - the count and
  the id coincide there - so a run without a respawn produces the same
  transcript as before and no recorded corpus moved.
  `test/sim-multiworker.test.js` drives a flap and fails on the id-derived
  form.

- **One unreadable cgroup file no longer pins the memory signal to a looser
  wall.** Limit discovery walks the process's own group and its ancestors and
  keeps the tightest limit, but it latched any finite result outright - so a
  transient read failure on the NEARER group's file (an EACCES tick, a
  remount) while a looser ancestor answered pinned that ancestor for the life
  of the process. The reader then measured the resident set against a wall
  several times larger than the one the kernel would actually kill on, and the
  MEMORY signal sat low while the worker walked into an out-of-memory death it
  was supposed to predict - a container with a 1 GiB limit under an 8 GiB
  parent reported a quarter while sitting at twice its own ceiling. Latching
